title: Mock 2 · Building Blocks
blurb: SIF strategy limits, cut-offs and tax, plus first numericals in futures, options and bonds.

questions.q: An investor keeps buying the same sector fund simply because 'everyone in my office is buying it'. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Behavioural biases distort decisions; herd mentality means copying others' investment actions.
hints: Correct — following the crowd rather than one's own analysis is herding.
Wrong — anchoring is fixating on an initial reference number.
Wrong — loss aversion is feeling losses more than equal gains.
Wrong — mental accounting is treating money differently by its source or label.

questions.q: Under the SIF 'Equity Ex-Top 100 Long-Short Fund' strategy, at least what portion of NAV must be invested in equity of stocks excluding the top 100 by market capitalisation?
questions.explanation: Ex-Top 100 Long-Short: min 65% of NAV in equity of non-top-100 stocks; unhedged short in non-large-caps capped at 25% of NAV.
hints: Wrong — 80% applies to Equity Long-Short and Sector Rotation strategies.
Correct — the floor is 65% of NAV outside the top 100 stocks.
Wrong — 50% is not the prescribed floor.
Wrong — 75% is the maximum sector exposure in the Sectoral Debt strategy.

questions.q: The SIF Debt Long-Short and Sectoral Debt Long-Short strategies must be structured as:
options: Close-ended schemes with no redemption until maturity
Interval schemes, with redemption allowed once a week or less frequently
Interval schemes with redemption twice a week
questions.explanation: Debt-oriented SIF strategies are interval schemes; AMCs may allow redemption once a week or at any lesser frequency.
hints: Wrong — only equity SIF strategies may be open-ended.
Wrong — they are interval, not close-ended.
Correct — both debt strategies are interval schemes; AMC may allow weekly or less frequent redemption.
Wrong — twice a week applies to the hybrid strategies.

questions.q: In the three-tier structure of a mutual fund, who appoints the custodian?
questions.explanation: Custodians register under SEBI (Custodian) Regulations 1996 and are appointed by the trustees.
hints: Wrong — the sponsor sets up the trust but does not appoint the custodian.
Wrong — the fund manager only manages investments.
Wrong — AMFI is an industry body, not an appointing authority.
Correct — the custodian is appointed by the trustees under a custodial agreement.

questions.q: For how long may an AMC use the sponsor's or mutual fund's brand name in the offer documents and advertisements of its SIF?
options: Three years from the first NFO of the SIF
Five years from the date of SEBI's approval for launch of the SIF
Indefinitely, as long as the font is smaller
questions.explanation: SIF must have its own name and logo; the MF/sponsor brand can be used for 5 years from SEBI approval, in a font no larger than the SIF brand.
hints: Wrong — the period is five years from SEBI approval.
Correct — the 5-year window helps the new SIF brand gain recognition.
Wrong — the permission is time-bound.
Wrong — it is permitted, with conditions such as 'brought to you by'.

questions.q: As on which dates must an SIF disclose its portfolio?
options: The last day of every month
The last day of each quarter only
The last day of every alternate month — May, July, September, November, January and March
Only as on 31 March and 30 September
questions.explanation: SIF portfolios are disclosed as on the last day of every alternate month (May, Jul, Sep, Nov, Jan, Mar) on AMC and AMFI websites within 10 days, with ISINs.
hints: Wrong — monthly disclosure applies to MF schemes.
Wrong — quarter-end alone is not the rule.
Correct — SIF portfolio disclosure is bi-monthly, within 10 days.
Wrong — half-yearly alone is not the rule for SIF.

questions.q: For an open-ended equity-oriented scheme, the maximum total expense ratio on the first ₹500 crore of daily net assets is:
questions.explanation: Base TER slab on the first ₹500 crore: 2.10% (equity-oriented) and 1.85% (others).
hints: Correct — the 2026 slab is 2.10% for equity-oriented schemes.
Wrong — 1.85% is the limit for other-than-equity schemes.
Wrong — 2.25% was an older limit.
Wrong — 1.00% is the cap for close-ended equity schemes.

questions.q: Ritu earns long-term capital gains of ₹2,00,000 from equity-oriented funds in a financial year (no other LTCG). What is her LTCG tax before cess and surcharge?
questions.explanation: Equity LTCG is taxed at 12.5% above the ₹1.25 lakh annual exemption: 75,000 × 12.5% = ₹9,375.
hints: Wrong — that ignores the ₹1.25 lakh exemption.
Wrong — that applies 20% (the STCG rate) to the excess.
Wrong — only the first ₹1.25 lakh is exempt.

questions.q: What is the cut-off time for purchases in a liquid fund?
questions.explanation: Liquid and overnight funds: purchase cut-off 1.30 pm; the previous day's NAV applies if funds are available before cut-off.
hints: Wrong — 3.00 pm applies to non-liquid purchases and to redemptions.
Wrong — noon is not a prescribed cut-off.
Correct — liquid and overnight fund purchases have a 1.30 pm cut-off.
Wrong — 7.00 pm applies to online redemptions in overnight funds.

questions.q: Within how many business days of the closure of an NFO must units be allotted or money refunded?
questions.explanation: Allot units or refund within 5 business days of NFO closure; delayed refunds attract 15% p.a. interest borne by the AMC.
hints: Wrong — 2 working days applies to demat conversion requests.
Correct — allotment/refund is due within 5 business days of NFO closure.
Wrong — 10 days is not the rule.
Wrong — 15 days is the maximum NFO period.

questions.q: A scheme returned 12% when the risk-free rate was 6% and the scheme's standard deviation was 4%. What is its Sharpe ratio?
questions.explanation: Sharpe ratio = (Rs − Rf) ÷ SD = 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5.
hints: Wrong — 12 ÷ 4 ignores the risk-free rate.
Wrong — that inverts the ratio.
Wrong — not supported by the data.

questions.q: Which investor profile is most suitable for an SIF Equity Long-Short strategy?
options: A retiree needing assured monthly income from ₹3 lakh
A first-time investor starting a ₹5,000 SIP
An investor seeking capital protection for an emergency fund
An investor with ₹15 lakh surplus, high risk appetite and understanding of short positions
questions.explanation: SIFs are riskier than MF schemes and require ₹10 lakh minimum; suitability requires high risk capacity and appetite.
hints: Wrong — below the ₹10 lakh threshold and needs income certainty.
Wrong — does not meet the ₹10 lakh threshold.
Wrong — emergency money needs safety and liquidity.
Correct — SIF needs ₹10 lakh+ and tolerance for the higher risk of long-short strategies.

questions.q: Exchange-traded derivatives trading in India began in June 2000 with:
questions.explanation: Sequence: index futures (Jun 2000) → index options (Jun 2001) → stock options (Jul 2001) → stock futures (Nov 2001).
hints: Wrong — stock options started in July 2001.
Wrong — index options started in June 2001.
Correct — index futures on Nifty and Sensex started in June 2000.
Wrong — stock futures started in November 2001.

questions.q: Impact cost of a stock is likely to be high when:
options: Liquidity in the stock is poor
Liquidity in the stock is very high
The order size is very small
The bid-ask spread is very narrow
questions.explanation: Impact cost is the percentage degradation from the ideal price; it rises with order size and falls with liquidity.
hints: Correct — thin order books push large orders far from the ideal price.
Wrong — high liquidity lowers impact cost.
Wrong — small orders face only the spread.
Wrong — a narrow spread signals liquidity and lower cost.

questions.q: Nifty spot is 24,894 and the near-month Nifty futures trade at 25,006. Using the workbook's definition, the basis is:
questions.explanation: Basis = Spot − Futures. Futures > spot ⇒ negative basis ⇒ contango.
hints: Wrong — basis is spot minus futures, so it is negative here.
Correct — basis = spot − futures = 24,894 − 25,006 = −112; futures above spot is contango.
Wrong — backwardation has spot above futures (positive basis).
Wrong — basis reaches zero only at expiry.

questions.q: Open interest in a futures contract refers to:
options: The number of contracts traded during the day
The total of long plus short positions
The margin money held by the clearing corporation
The total number of contracts outstanding (counted on one side)
questions.explanation: Open interest = contracts yet to be settled; number of longs = number of shorts = OI.
hints: Wrong — that is traded volume.
Wrong — longs always equal shorts, so only one side is counted.
Wrong — margin is unrelated to OI.
Correct — OI counts outstanding contracts, only one side.

questions.q: XYZ shares trade at ₹1,286. A ₹1,250 strike call is quoted at ₹60. What is the call's intrinsic value?
questions.explanation: Call intrinsic value = max(S − X, 0) = ₹36; time value = 60 − 36 = ₹24.
hints: Wrong — ₹60 is the full premium.
Correct — intrinsic value = S − X = 1,286 − 1,250.
Wrong — ₹24 is the time value (60 − 36).
Wrong — the call is in-the-money, so intrinsic value is positive.

questions.q: A stock trades at ₹940. A ₹900 strike put is priced at ₹12. How much of the premium is time value?
questions.explanation: For OTM options the entire premium is time value. Put intrinsic value = max(X − S, 0) = 0.
hints: Wrong — ₹40 is spot minus strike, not a put value.
Wrong — ₹52 adds unrelated numbers.
Wrong — an unexpired option always has time value.
Correct — the put is OTM (strike < spot), so intrinsic value is zero and the whole premium is time value.

questions.q: A trader expects a big move in a stock after a court verdict but is unsure of the direction. Which strategy suits this view?
questions.explanation: Long straddle = long call + long put, same strike and expiry; a view on volatility, not direction.
hints: Correct — buying a call and a put at the same strike profits from a large move either way.
Wrong — a short straddle profits only if the price stays stable.
Wrong — a covered call is mildly bullish/neutral income generation.
Wrong — a bull spread needs a rise.

questions.q: A covered call (long stock + short call) has a payoff similar to:
questions.explanation: Covered call = synthetic short put; protective put = synthetic long call.
hints: Wrong — a protective put resembles a long call.
Wrong — a long put profits from falls.
Correct — it caps upside and leaves downside open — the shape of a short put.
Wrong — a straddle profits from big moves.

questions.q: For a zero-coupon bond, Macaulay duration is:
options: Less than its time to maturity
Equal to its time to maturity
Greater than its time to maturity
questions.explanation: Zero-coupon bonds have no interim cash flows, so duration equals maturity.
hints: Wrong — coupon bonds have duration below maturity.
Correct — with a single cash flow at maturity, the weighted average time is the maturity.
Wrong — duration cannot exceed maturity for an option-free bond.
Wrong — duration is zero only at maturity.

questions.q: The tick size for cash-settled GOI bond futures is ₹0.0025. What is the change in contract value per tick for one lot?
questions.explanation: Tick value = lot (2,000) × tick (₹0.0025) = ₹5 per lot.
hints: Correct — 2,000 bonds × ₹0.0025 = ₹5.
Wrong — that ignores the 2,000-bond lot.
Wrong — ₹1.25 is the tick value of 91-day T-bill futures.
Wrong — that uses 20,000 bonds.

questions.q: Which option pricing model is used in India for computing theoretical prices of exchange-traded interest rate options on government securities?
questions.explanation: The workbook states Black 1976 is used for theoretical prices of exchange-traded IROs in India.
hints: Wrong — the binomial model is iterative and not the stated model.
Wrong — Black-Scholes uses spot prices; Black-76 replaces spot with discounted futures.
Correct — Black-76 uses futures/forward prices and is applied to IROs.
Wrong — parity is a relationship, not a pricing model.

questions.q: A bond portfolio manager expects interest rates to rise. Using GOI bond futures, the manager should:
options: Do nothing, as futures cannot hedge rates
questions.explanation: Rate-rise view: sell GOI bond futures / buy bond puts / sell T-bill futures / buy MIBOR futures.
hints: Wrong — long futures lose when rates rise.
Wrong — calls gain when bond prices rise (rates fall).
Wrong — bond futures are designed for rate hedging.
Correct — rising rates lower bond prices, so a short futures position gains.

questions.q: An insurance company expects large premium inflows next month and fears that interest rates will fall before it can invest. It should:
options: Buy GOI bond futures (a long hedge)
questions.explanation: Long hedge: buy futures to lock in purchase price/yield when you will invest later and fear falling rates.
hints: Correct — a long hedge locks today's yield for future investment.
Wrong — selling protects existing holdings against a rate rise.
Wrong — long MIBOR futures gain when rates rise.
Wrong — selling calls gives limited premium and loses if prices rise.
